title: Pet Carbon Footprint Calculator: Dog & Cat CO₂ per Year
h1: Pet Carbon Footprint Calculator — Dogs & Cats
description: Pet carbon footprint calculator for dogs and cats: enter weight to see annual kg of CO₂ (a 10 kg dog ≈ 1,200 kg/yr) plus the trees needed to offset. Free.
answerSnippet: A 10 kg dog emits roughly 1,200 kg CO₂/year; a 10 kg cat emits about 900 kg CO₂/year. The main source is meat-based pet food. To offset: each tree absorbs ~22 kg CO₂/year, so a 10 kg dog needs about 55 trees.
intro: Pets are surprisingly carbon-intensive — mostly because of the meat in commercial pet food. A 15 kg dog can emit as much CO₂ in a year as driving roughly 7,000 km. This calculator gives you the annual CO₂ equivalent for your dog or cat based on body weight, plus the number of trees needed to offset it. All calculations follow standard lifecycle emission factors used in peer-reviewed sustainability research.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **CO₂_dog ≈ weight (kg) × 120 kg CO₂/year**; **CO₂_cat ≈ weight (kg) × 90 kg CO₂/year**. Food (meat-based kibble) accounts for ~70% of a dog's footprint. A 4 kg cat emits ~360 kg CO₂/year; a 30 kg dog emits ~3,600 kg CO₂/year.
useCases: Estimating your household's true carbon footprint (including pets)
Deciding how many trees to plant or carbon credits to buy
Comparing the footprint of dogs vs cats before adopting
Evaluating the impact of switching to lower-carbon pet food

explanation:
## How much CO₂ does a pet emit per year?

For a **dog**, annual CO₂ emissions ≈ **body weight (kg) × 120**. For a **cat**, annual CO₂ emissions ≈ **body weight (kg) × 90**. These factors derive from lifecycle analysis of commercial meat-based pet food production and distribution, primarily referenced in Okin (2017, *PLOS ONE*) and subsequent studies by the University of Edinburgh (2020).

---

### How this calculator works

The formula uses **body weight as a proxy for food consumption**, since caloric intake scales predictably with mass in domestic mammals. The CO₂-equivalent figures (CO₂e) incorporate not just carbon dioxide but also methane and nitrous oxide from livestock production — converted to a single number using 100-year global warming potentials (GWP100). One kilogram of beef protein generates roughly **27–30 kg CO₂e**; chicken protein generates around **6–8 kg CO₂e**. Standard commercial kibble blends both, which is why the per-kg multipliers used here are conservative averages rather than best- or worst-case figures.

The "trees to offset" figure assumes **one mature tree absorbs approximately 22 kg CO₂ per year** — a widely cited mean based on temperate-zone forest species. Tropical trees can absorb more; urban ornamental trees often absorb less.

---

### Quick reference table

| Pet & weight | CO₂e/year | CO₂e/year (t) | Trees to offset |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cat 4 kg | 360 kg | 0.4 t | 17 |
| Cat 6 kg | 540 kg | 0.5 t | 25 |
| Small dog 5 kg | 600 kg | 0.6 t | 28 |
| Medium dog 15 kg | 1,800 kg | 1.8 t | 82 |
| Large dog 30 kg | 3,600 kg | 3.6 t | 164 |
| Giant dog 50 kg | 6,000 kg | 6.0 t | 273 |

For context: the average annual carbon footprint of a person in Spain is approximately **5.7 t CO₂e** (Eurostat, 2022). A large dog at 30 kg reaches roughly **63% of that figure**.

---

### What drives the footprint?

- **Meat-based pet food: ~70–80%** of total emissions. Commercial kibble is calorie-dense in animal protein. Beef-heavy formulas carry the highest footprint; poultry- or fish-based formulas are significantly lower. Wet food (cans, pouches) tends to have a higher footprint per calorie than dry kibble due to packaging and lower energy density.
- **Veterinary care: ~10–15%**. Manufacturing pharmaceuticals, anaesthetic gases, transport, and facility energy. Some anaesthetic agents (e.g. isoflurane, sevoflurane) are potent greenhouse gases themselves, though their contribution at the individual pet level is marginal.
- **Accessories & waste disposal: ~5–10%**. Single-use plastic waste bags, synthetic toys, and non-recyclable bedding are the main contributors here. A US household with dogs uses an estimated **900+ plastic bags per year** for waste alone.

---

### What this calculator does NOT include

- **Country of origin of pet food ingredients.** A kibble manufactured with South American beef has a different transport footprint than one using local poultry. This calculator uses global averages.
- **Raw or home-cooked diets.** If your pet eats primarily raw beef, the actual footprint will be substantially higher than this estimate. If they eat primarily plant-based or insect-based food, it will be lower.
- **Breeding and acquisition.** The carbon cost of professional breeding operations (facilities, transport, health screening) is real but highly variable and is not included here.
- **End-of-life.** Pet cremation emits roughly **15–30 kg CO₂** per animal; burial has near-zero direct emissions but is excluded from most lifecycle studies.

---

### Common mistakes when reading pet footprint data

1. **Confusing CO₂ with CO₂e.** Most credible studies report in CO₂-equivalent, which includes methane from livestock — a gas with 28× the warming effect of CO₂ over 100 years. Headlines that strip out the "e" understate the real impact.
2. **Assuming all kibble is equal.** Protein source matters enormously. Switching from a beef-first to a chicken-first kibble of the same weight can reduce food emissions by up to **40%** without changing portion size.
3. **Overestimating tree offsets.** A tree planted today will not reach peak absorption for 10–20 years. The "trees needed" figure here represents a steady-state offset target, not an immediate fix.

---

### Practical ways to reduce your pet's footprint

1. **Switch protein source before switching volume.** Choosing poultry, fish, or insect-based kibble over beef-based formulas is the highest-impact single change available. Insect protein (e.g. black soldier fly) generates roughly **1–2 kg CO₂e per kg protein** — versus 27+ kg for beef.
2. **Prefer dry food over wet food** when nutritionally appropriate for your pet, due to higher energy density and lower packaging waste per calorie.
3. **Replace single-use plastic waste bags** with certified compostable alternatives or newspaper wrapping where local regulations allow.
4. **Use the tree count as a concrete annual target** — verified reforestation programs (e.g. those certified under the Gold Standard or Verra VCS) report actual absorption rates per species and region.
5. **Adopt, don't shop** — rescue animals avoid the direct carbon and resource cost of professional breeding facilities.

faq.q: How many kg of CO₂ does a dog produce per year?
faq.a: It depends on body weight. A 15 kg dog emits roughly 1,800 kg CO₂/year (1.8 t), mainly from meat-based kibble. A 30 kg dog emits ~3,600 kg/year. The formula is: CO₂ = weight (kg) × 120.

faq.q: Is a dog's carbon footprint bigger than a cat's?
faq.a: Yes. Dogs typically emit more CO₂ because they are heavier and eat more meat-based food. A 15 kg dog emits ~1,800 kg CO₂/year; a 5 kg cat emits ~450 kg CO₂/year. Per kg of body weight, dogs (×120) also have a higher factor than cats (×90) because dog food contains a higher proportion of meat.

faq.q: How does my pet's carbon footprint compare to a person's?
faq.a: The global average human carbon footprint is about 4–5 t CO₂/year. A 15 kg dog at 1.8 t/year represents about 35–45% of one person's footprint. A 5 kg cat (450 kg/year) is roughly 10% of a person's annual emissions.

faq.q: How many trees do I need to offset my dog's CO₂?
faq.a: One mature tree absorbs approximately 22 kg of CO₂ per year. To offset a 15 kg dog (1,800 kg CO₂/year), you would need to plant about 82 trees. This calculator shows the exact number for your pet's weight.

faq.q: Can I reduce my pet's footprint by switching to vegan pet food?
faq.a: Yes. Vegan or insect-protein pet food can cut food-related emissions by 50–80%. Nutritionally balanced vegan dog food is available and recognized by veterinary associations in several countries, though you should check with your vet before making the switch.

faq.q: Does pet waste contribute to carbon emissions?
faq.a: Yes, though it is a smaller factor than food. Pet waste in landfills decomposes anaerobically and produces methane (a potent greenhouse gas). Composting pet waste away from water sources or using biodegradable bags reduces this impact.

faq.q: Is adopting a rescue pet more eco-friendly than buying from a breeder?
faq.a: Yes. Rescue adoption skips the energy and resources needed for breeding, neonatal care, and transport. It also reduces demand for industrial breeding operations, which carry a higher per-animal carbon cost.

faq.q: Why does pet food have such a large carbon footprint?
faq.a: Meat production is one of the most carbon-intensive food processes on Earth. Commercial pet food is largely meat-based — raising livestock for pet food requires land (often via deforestation), water, and fossil fuels, all of which generate CO₂ and methane. A study by UCLA researcher Gregory Okin (2017) estimated that US cats and dogs together produce 64 Mt of CO₂e per year.

The factors (120 kg CO₂/kg for dogs, 90 kg CO₂/kg for cats) are based on lifecycle analyses from peer-reviewed research. Individual results vary by brand of pet food, local energy mix, and lifestyle. Treat these as reliable order-of-magnitude estimates, not precise measurements.
